notes: Stopped: the four parallel simulations ran in lockstep, and a step that skipped through a quiet spell made the others wait, so it ran at about 16 decisions a second (17 hours for a million). Skipping is now capped per step; replaced by stage1a-02. Its head start agreed with the speed-only controller 89% of the time.

Tested at 100k decisions on 40 unseen sessions against the speed-only rules controller: 83 separation losses against 81, 64 gaps inside the minimum against 41, 0 speed instructions. Its best choice was always 'leave the speed alone': the head start copied a controller that leaves speeds alone about 9 times in 10. No speed control did almost as well on separation, so most losses come from the planner releasing aircraft only about 4 NM apart. Replaced by stage1a-03: speeds chosen as targets, a weighted head start, and more room from the planner.

Target speeds (160-250 kt in 10 kt values, inside the band) instead of steps; head start weighted towards speed changes; planner slots about 4.5 NM apart with fixed paths. The machine was restarted at about 19:00, 181k decisions in; resumed from the 100k copy (the 81k decisions in between are set aside), so 4.6 hours includes about 0.4 hours lost. Tested on 40 unseen sessions against the speed-only rules controller (56 separation losses, gap error 2.44 NM, 3.9 instructions per arrival): head start 46 / 2.36 / 3.6, 100k 52 / 2.41 / 3.7, 300k 97 / 2.68 / 3.9, 500k 53 / 2.51 / 4.1, 750k 53 / 2.44 / 4.3, final 52 / 2.36 / 4.7. Gate not passed; up to about 20 losses either way is within the noise of 40 sessions. Practice made it more random (chance of its top choice 95% after the head start, 57% at the end) and no better.

Holding stacks like real ones (first come first served, lowest leaves first, levels only once vacated, climb out of a taken level); only aircraft whose speed the AI gives count in its action probabilities and uncertainty; uncertainty reward 0.001; fading penalty (0.5 to 0.05) for moving away from the head start.
